sources.locator: §2.7 'Interval structure', printed pp. 48–55 (PDF pp. 57–64), and Appendix A2.2–A2.4, printed pp. 300–304, read in full; §2.8, Appendix A2.1, A2.5 and the exercises were not read

contents.name: §2.7 rooted deletion labeling of the maximal chains of a Bruhat interval by positions deleted from a fixed reduced word, with Example 2.7.1 (the four maximal chains of the S3 interval and their label words (1,2,3), (1,3,2), (3,1,2), (3,2,1))
Lemma 2.7.2: at most one maximal chain of an interval has a strictly increasing label word
Lemma 2.7.3: every rank-two Bruhat interval is a diamond, with exactly two maximal chains, one increasing and one decreasing
contents.reason: The abstract replacement argument replaces a two-step segment by the increasing chain of the rooted rank-two interval and needs no diamond classification of rank-two intervals; the Bruhat-specific isomorphism is not consumed by any item of this pair.

contents.name: Lemma 2.7.4: the increasing maximal chain exists in every closed quotient interval [u,w]_J and is lexicographically first
Theorem 2.7.5: the order complex of (u,w)_J is shellable, by the first-divergence and first-reunion replacement of a descending two-step segment
Corollary 2.7.6: the order complex of (u,w)_J is Cohen-Macaulay
contents.reason: No page of this run claims Cohen-Macaulayness of an order complex, and the pair stops at the combinatorial facet criterion of a shelling together with the Moebius formula.

contents.name: Theorem 2.7.7: the order complex of the open interval is PL homeomorphic to a sphere (full intervals) or a ball
contents.reason: The pair claims shellability and the Moebius value, not the PL sphere/ball homeomorphism; the resolution of intervals by reflection subgroups needed for that theorem is not developed on this page.

contents.name: Corollary 2.7.8 and Example 2.7.9: length-three Bruhat intervals are k-crowns, and arbitrarily large crowns occur in infinite Coxeter groups
contents.reason: These classify the poset shapes of rank-three Bruhat intervals; no item or consumer of this pair uses the k-crown classification.

contents.name: Corollary 2.7.10: the quotient Moebius value mu_J(u,w) is (-1)^ell for full intervals and 0 otherwise
contents.reason: The approved full-interval Mobius and parity statements are proved at thm-cg-bruhat-eulerian-intervals-and-mobius on batch16. The grouped parabolic-quotient Mobius formula is not a selected supplier promise: batch16 explicitly supplies a quotient counterexample to extending the full Eulerian formula indiscriminately. This abstract pair proves only the general falling-chain formula; no unproved quotient specialization is asserted by this deferral.

contents.name: Corollary 2.7.11: in a closed interval of length > 0 the odd-length and even-length elements are equinumerous
contents.reason: Rank-parity balance of nontrivial full Bruhat intervals is proved and promised at thm-cg-bruhat-eulerian-intervals-and-mobius, Statement (1), on batch16. This abstract finite-poset pair proves the general falling-chain formula, not the Bruhat specialization.

contents.name: Theorem 2.7.12, Example 2.7.13 and Corollary 2.7.14: the regular CW model of the open interval, its cellular boundary and the balanced signature/cellular chain complex
contents.reason: The pair does not build regular CW models of intervals, cellular boundaries or balanced signatures; the design keeps these out of the authored scope.

contents.name: Appendix A2.2: partial orders, lattices, the Moebius recursion (A2.1) and the incidence algebra
Appendix A2.3: the order complex of a poset, its faces as chains
Fact A2.3.1: the Moebius value mu(x,y) equals the reduced Euler characteristic of the order complex of the open interval
contents.reason: The pair derives the falling-chain formula from the published interval recurrence and the flag f-vector, not from the Euler characteristic of a complex; the topological identity is not consumed.

contents.name: Definition A2.4.1 and its equivalence: shelling as a linear order of facets in which each facet meets the union of the earlier ones in a pure (d-1)-dimensional complex, equivalently the pairwise facet replacement condition, and (A2.4) preservation of shellability under coning

(A2.5) the restriction of a facet, (A2.6) the h-vector as the distribution of restriction sizes, and Facts A2.4.2-A2.4.6 (restriction characterization, PL balls and spheres, wedge-of-spheres homotopy type, Cohen-Macaulayness, colored complexes)
contents.reason: The falling-chain formula is proved on this page through the flag f-vector and the Moebius recurrence; the restriction map, the complex h-vector, the wedge-of-spheres homotopy type and the Cohen-Macaulay applications are not consumed by this pair or its consumers.

sources.title: Michelle L. Wachs, Poset topology: tools and applications (IAS/Park City Mathematics Institute lectures 2004; arXiv:math/0602226)
sources.locator: Lecture 3, §§3.1–3.4, printed pp. 41–66 (PDF pp. 43–68), read in full; Lectures 1–2 and 4 onwards were not read

contents.name: §3.1 definition of a shellable complex and Theorem 3.1.3 with Corollary 3.1.4: shellable complexes have the homotopy type of a wedge of spheres and reduced homology Z^{r_i} for the homology facets
contents.reason: The pair proves the combinatorial facet criterion and the Moebius formula, and claims no homotopy type or homology; the sphere decomposition is not consumed.

contents.name: §3.2 Definition 3.2.1: EL-labeling (edge labels, unique increasing maximal chain in every closed interval, lexicographically first)
§3.2 Theorem 3.2.2: for an EL-labeling the lexicographic order of the maximal chains is a shelling of the order complex
§3.2 Theorem 3.2.4: the number of i-spheres equals the number of decreasing maximal (i+2)-chains, and these chains give a cohomology basis
contents.reason: The pair recovers only the Moebius consequence of the falling-chain count, from the recurrence and the flag f-vector; no wedge-of-spheres statement, cohomology basis or chain-level algebra is claimed here.

contents.name: §3.2 Remark 3.2.5: the weak and strict variants of EL-labelings and their known non-equivalence in general
§3.3 Definition 3.3.1: CL-labeling (chain-edge labels, rooted intervals, unique increasing chain lexicographically first)
§3.3 Theorem 3.3.4: the dual CL-labeling of Bruhat order on a quotient W^J, with exactly one decreasing chain when J is empty and at most one otherwise
contents.reason: The Bruhat deletion labeling and its decreasing chains are the proof home of the Bruhat-interval shelling page of this run, which consumes the general criterion and Moebius formula proved on this page.

contents.name: §3.3 Corollary 3.3.5: every open Bruhat quotient interval is homeomorphic to a sphere or a ball
contents.reason: The pair does not claim the sphere/ball homeomorphism type of open intervals, only the combinatorial shelling criterion and the Moebius value.

contents.name: §3.4 the descent set of a maximal chain of a pure poset with a CL-labeling
§3.4 Theorem 3.4.1: rank-selected subposets of pure CL-shellable posets are CL-shellable and have the homotopy type of a wedge of spheres, one per chain with the given descent set
contents.reason: The rank-selection theorem is a homotopy-type statement about rank-selected subposets; the pair uses only the descent set of a maximal chain and the Moebius value of an interval.

contents.name: Lecture 4 §4.1 Lemma 4.4: Philip Hall's chain-sum formula mu(0hat,1hat) = -c_1 + c_2 - c_3 + ... over chains of the bounded poset
Lecture 4 §4.1 Definition 4.11: E-labeling (unique weakly increasing saturated chain in every interval)
Lecture 4 §4.1 Theorem 4.11 with its proof: (-1)^{rk(x,y)} mu(x,y) equals the number of strictly decreasing saturated chains, via the flag f-vector claim, the flag h-vector and Lemma 4.4
Lecture 4 §4.1 Theorem 4.12: the broken circuit theorem expressing coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of a matroid by the broken circuit complex

sources.title: Nathan Reading, Lattice congruences of the weak order: algebra, combinatorics, and geometry (Triangle Lectures in Combinatorics, Wake Forest University, 30 March 2019), slides
sources.locator: The 'Lattice congruences for combinatorialists' part, slides 2–9 (lattices, homomorphisms, congruences, quotients, the order-theoretic characterization and the quotient caveats); the later sections of the deck were not read

contents.name: Order-theoretic characterization of a lattice congruence: an equivalence relation on a finite lattice is a congruence if and only if every class is an interval and the maps to the least and greatest element of the class are order-preserving
Quotient construction [x] v [y] = [x v y], [x] ^ [y] = [x ^ y] for a congruence, with the induced lattice order on classes
The set of least elements of congruence classes is a lattice isomorphic to the quotient, is a join-sublattice of L, and can fail to be a sublattice
contents.reason: The general quotient lattice and monotone interval endpoints are proved locally by lem-cg-lattice-quotient-descent-and-class-intervals and thm-cg-finite-lattice-interval-congruence-criterion. The specific sortable-image sublattice is proved on batch32 by thm-cg-sortable-meet-join-closure-and-cambrian-quotient. A general congruence image being an ambient join-sublattice, or failing to be an ambient sublattice, is not inferred from that special case or added as a promise by this grouped source deferral.

contents.name: Lattice homomorphisms, congruences and quotients for finite lattices, and the take-home test: check the fibres are intervals, then check the two endpoint maps
